papers.title: Notes on Generative AI for Mathematical Research
papers.abstract: These notes describe how generative AI is now used to solve and to check research-level mathematics, with a focus on agents and their harnesses. For the proving agents Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos and the verification agent OSVerify, we explain the design principles, compare each with its base model, present case studies, and show how to use and contribute to them. We also briefly review the history of AI for mathematics and the community's reactions to it.

papers.title: Notes on an elementary proof of Weil II from Hexagon
papers.abstract: Recently, L. Alp\"oge sketched an elementary proof of Deligne's weight bound in footnote 3 of his remark on joint work with Claude on the Riemann hypothesis. An expanded, AI-generated account appeared on Hexagon, where it was posted by F. Alderliefste. This note gives an exposition of the proof presented there.

papers.title: Louis Bachelier's Theorie de la speculation: Circulation and Reception
papers.abstract: Louis Bachelier's Theorie de la speculation (1900) introduced a probabilistic model of Brownian motion in a study of financial fluctuations, five years before Einstein's physical theory. By connecting probability distributions with the heat equation and studying speculation and option valuation, Bachelier anticipated central developments in probability, physics, and mathematical finance. How widely did the thesis circulate before its broader significance was recognized? Drawing on library correspondence, surviving copies, accession registers, provenance marks, historical catalogues, and acquisition lists, this article reconstructs its international circulation and reception in two forms: the separate Gauthier-Villars dissertation and its publication in the Annales scientifiques de l'Ecole normale superieure. It identifies thirty-eight foreign academic institutions in the official dissertation exchange network for 1900 and documents its operation. University exchanges, commercial purchases, journal distribution, and personal presentations provided complementary channels. American holdings reveal its geographical reach, including receipt at Cornell in April 1900. Contemporary reviews and subsequent uses establish selective engagement in mathematics, actuarial science, and economics, including transmission without attribution. An examination of probability composition and diffusion clarifies the thesis's place in the history of stochastic processes and its relationship to physical Brownian motion. Columbia's journal volume, accessioned in 1901 and borrowed by Mandelbrot in 1961, connects early dissemination with renewed interest. Distinguishing availability from documented reading and use, the study shows that delayed recognition coexisted with early international circulation and a dispersed readership across scientific traditions.

papers.title: Questions, Explanation and Synthesis in Service Mathematics: Course Design with Didactic Units and Hybrid Teaching
papers.abstract: Students may have access to a convincing mathematical explanation without being able to reconstruct or adapt it. A course must provide opportunities to develop that understanding while keeping the work sustainable for students and teachers. This article develops a methodology for service mathematics in which a question ledger guides both course authoring and classroom decisions. Course-relative didactic units organise explanatory purposes, prerequisites and connections, initially calibrated by a five-to-seven-minute expert account. Teaching combines preparation, student exposition and supported repair with substantial teacher exposition and synthesis. Their allocation changes with the topic, audience and conditions of teaching. Compression and recovery explain how developed constructions become reusable while their grounds remain accessible. Three analyses from mathematics for computing-full Sudoku encoding, grayscale projection and a software failure contract-show how contrasting cases guide explanation and revision. The practice-informed contribution connects coherent course design with adaptable teaching and manageable preparation, and identifies questions for evaluating learning, participation and sustained teacher effort.

papers.title: The Role of Mathematicians in Mathematics
papers.abstract: Some reflections on the role of mathematicians in an age of proofs found and verified by machines.

papers.title: On the number theory of the Greeks. I. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
papers.abstract: In this article we present Euclid's fundamental theorem of number theory and give evidence for the claim that this theorem, which is largely unknown today, was as familiar to number theorists before Gauss as the Gaussian version of the fundamental theorem is to us.

papers.title: On the Number Theory of the Greeks. II. Gauss's Lemmas and Riesz Domains
papers.abstract: In the second part of our article on Euclid's four number theorem we start from the notion of incommensurability and take a closer look at irrationality proofs for algebraic numbers. Along the way we encounter Gauss's Lemma, integral closure and Dedekind's Prague theorem, and finally we arrive back at the four number theorem.

papers.title: One machine, three drawings: a didactic analysis of a teaching progression for the function concept from Grade 4 to Grade 10
papers.abstract: The function concept can be entered through a correspondence between sets, a relation that is single-valued, or through a process that turns an input into an output. This paper presents the design rationale and a critical analysis of a source progression for functions (Grades 4-10, nominal ages 9-16, with two levels on relations between quantities), from which French-curriculum and International Baccalaureate chapters published at https://commeunjeu.org are assembled. One schema is presented first and kept throughout: a function is a machine that takes an input, applies a rule and gives exactly one output. Its drawing changes with age (a robot, then a box, then the arrow $f : x \mapsto f(x)$), and each change is shown once, the two drawings side by side; after 15 the box returns only in the lessons, to explain composition and the inverse. The properties that research identifies as difficult (the uniqueness of the output, the constant function, the function without a formula, two rules for one function, preimages) are posed on the machine from Grade 4; the word relation is kept for the link between two quantities, where covariation is taught; the set of ordered pairs comes back as the graph. The choices are related to the function machine as a cognitive root and to its authors' own warnings, to process-object accounts, to studies of concept images and of covariation, and to the French and IB curricula. A block-level audit of the dated source documents found the machine in only 2 of the 177 exercise blocks of Grades 7 to 10, no exercise asking pupils to draw a machine, and public chapters that opened on the relation; the revisions made after the audit are recorded with their counts before and after. No empirical evaluation is reported; hypotheses for one are stated.

papers.title: Lessons from Chess: Mathematics in the Age of AI
papers.abstract: The history of chess offers a perspective on the growing role of artificial intelligence in mathematics. We explore the parallels and limitations of this analogy and consider possible directions for mathematical research, education, and the public perception of mathematics.

papers.title: A Calculus Gradient: Child Poverty, Mathematics Preparation, and First-Year College Performance at a Hispanic-Serving University
papers.abstract: The San Antonio metropolitan area has one of the highest poverty rates among large U.S. metropolitan areas. Within Bexar County, where the city is located, child poverty varies widely across school districts. We link entrants of the city's public research university, a broad-access Hispanic-Serving Institution, to their sending schools and districts, and examine their preparation scores and first-year outcomes. Across the nation's school districts, enrollment in widely taken core courses (Algebra II, Geometry, Biology) shows little relation to child poverty, while enrollment in Calculus and Advanced Placement mathematics and science is far lower where child poverty is higher, nationally and within Bexar County. Among linked entrants, mathematics preparation differs with the school and district. Entrants with stronger mathematics preparation earn higher first-year grades in nearly every subject. Most entrants who do not return after the first year had unsuccessful courses, and mathematics is the largest single source of those outcomes. Among students who change major, mathematics is one of the subjects with grades furthest below their own averages. Within the same course and term, larger mathematics sections go with more unsuccessful outcomes for entrants with lower mathematics preparation, which identifies a hypothesis for testing smaller sections. Recorded between Fall 2014 and Fall 2019, these outcomes offer a reference point for change after the pandemic, test-optional admissions, and generative artificial intelligence. The analysis is reproducible; adapting it elsewhere requires local definitions and linkage validation. All results are associations among the students of one institution; establishing causes would require a designed study.

papers.title: Alain Badiou's Mistake: Two Postulates of Dialectical Materialism
papers.abstract: Originally published in 2013, this revised article constitutes the first stage of a two-part intervention that revisits Alain Badiou's deployment of topos theory in Being and Event and Logics of Worlds. It interrogates the structural and philosophical consequences of taking the category-theoretic foundations of mathematics seriously, extending the formal boundaries of mathematical discourse. This part focuses on Logics of Worlds, which emerged as Badiou's response to his own theory of subjectivity. While revisiting structures implicit in his reading of Cohen's proof of the independence of the continuum hypothesis, I demonstrate how his concept of 'dialectical materialism' remains constrained by set-theoretic ontology and localic topos theory - essentially a theory of intuitionistic logic. In particular, Badiou's claim that categorical thinking does not substantially change mathematics overlooks the true geometric momentum driving topos theory. While the primary contents of this article are technical, I further explore how Badiou's formal omissions critically impact his philosophical project. This is especially visible in regard to his 'postulate of materialism' - a device he utilizes to promote dialectical materialism as a credible alternative to science. Through its category-theoretic reframing, I show that the postulate actually encapsulates two structurally different conditions, one of which directly constrains his own project while the other part captures a type of atomism juxtaposed with Badiou's condescending assessment of democracy. By leveraging such claims indebted to his pre-committed, logicist comprehension of mathematics, Badiou reinstitutes an absolutist Truth-doctrine and an ultimately despotic political program against a genuine concept of multiplicity. His errors thus hardly constitute merely an inadvertent formal slip, but indicate a deeper, political intent.
